source_text: PAX ecce, dilectissimi fratres, Ecclesiae reddita est et, quod difficile nuper incredulis ac perfidis impossibile videbatur, ope atque ultione divina securitas nostra reparata est. In laetitiam mentes redeunt, et, tempestate pressurae ac nube discussa, tranquillitas ac serenitas refulserunt. Dandae laudes Deo, et beneficia ejus ac munera cum gratiarum actione celebranda, quamvis agere gratias nostra vox nec in persecutione cessaverit. Neque enim tantum inimico licere potest ut non, qui Dominum toto corde et anima et virtute diligimus, benedictiones ejus et laudes semper et ubique cum gloria praedicemus. Exoptatus votis omnium dies venit, et, post longae noctis horribilem tetramque caliginem, Domini luce radiatus mundus eluxit. Confessores, praeconio boni nominis claros et virtutis ac fidei laudibus gloriosos, laetis conspectibus intuemur, sanctis osculis adhaerentes, desideratos diu inexplebili cupiditate complectimur. Adest militum Christi cohors candida, qui persecutionis urgentus ferociam turbulentam stabili congressione fregerunt, parati ad patientiam carceris, armati ad tolerantiam mortis. Repugnastis fortiter saeculo, spectaculum gloriosum praebuistis Deo, secuturis fratribus fuistis exemplo. Religiosa vox Christum locuta est, in quem se semel credidisse confessa est. Illustres manus, quae non nisi divinis operibus assueverant, sacrificiis sacrilegis restiterunt. Sanctificata ora coelestibus cibis, post corpus et sanguinem Domini, profana contagia et idolorum reliquias respuerunt. Ab impio sceleratoque velamine, quo illic velabantur sacrificantium capita captiva, caput vestrum liberum mansit. Frons cum signo Dei pura, diaboli coronam ferre non potuit, coronae se Domini reservavit. Quam vos laete sinu suo excipit mater Ecclesia de praelio revertentes! quam beata, quam gaudens portas suas aperit, ut adunatis agminibus intretis, de hoste prostrato trophaea referentes! Cum triumphantibus viris et feminae veniunt, quae cum saeculo dimicantes, sexum quoque vicerunt. Veniunt et geminata militiae suae gloria virgines, et pueri annos suos virtutibus transeuntes. Necnon et caetera stantium multitudo vestram gloriam sequitur, proximis et pene conjunctis laudis insignibus vestigia vestra comitatur. Eadem et in illis sinceritas cordis, eadem fidei tenacis integritas. Inconcussis praeceptorum coelestium radicibus nixos et evangelicis traditionibus roboratos, non praescripta exilia, non destinata tormenta, non rei familiaris damna, non corporis supplicia terruerunt. Explorandae fidei praefiniebantur dies. Sed qui saeculo renuntiasse se meminit, nullum saeculi diem novit; nec tempora terrena jam computat qui aeternitatem de Deo sperat. Nemo, fratres dilectissimi, nemo hanc gloriam mutilet, nemo incorruptam stantium firmitatem maligna obtrectatione debilitet. Cum dies negantibus praestitutus excessit, quisquis professus intra diem non est, Christianum se esse confessus est. Primus est victoriae titulus, gentilium manibus apprehensum Dominum confiteri: secundus ad gloriam gradus est cauta secessione subtractum Domino reservari. Illa publica, haec privata confessio est. Ille judicem saeculi vincit, hic contentus Deo suo judice conscientiam puram cordis integritate custodit. Illic, fortitudo promptior, hic sollicitudo securior. Ille appropinquante hora sua, jam maturus inventus est; hic fortasse dilatus est qui, patrimonio derelicto, idcirco secessit quia non erat negaturus: confiteretur utique si fuisset et ipse detentus. Has martyrum coelestes coronas, has confessorum glorias spiritales, has stantium fratrum maximas eximiasque virtutes moestitia una contristat, quod avulsam nostrorum viscerum partem violentus inimicus populationis suae strage dejecit. Quid hoc loco faciam, dilectissimi fratres? fluctuans vario mentis aestu, quid aut quomodo dicam? Lacrymis magis quam verbis opus est ad exprimendum dolorem quo corporis nostri plaga deflenda est, quo populi aliquando numerosi multiplex lamentanda jactura est. Quis enim sic durus aut ferreus, quis sic fraternae charitatis oblitus, qui inter suorum multiformes ruinas et lugubres ac multo squalore deformes reliquias constitutus siccos oculos tenere praevaleat, nec, erumpente statim fletu, prius gemitus suos lacrymis quam voce depromat? Doleo, fratres, doleo vobiscum, nec mihi ad leniendos dolores meos integritas propria et sanitas privata blanditur, quando plus pastor in gregis sui vulnere vulneretur. Cum singulis pectus meum copulo, moeroris et funeris pondera luctuosa participo. Cum plangentibus plango, cum deflentibus defleo, cum jacentibus jacere me credo. Jaculis illis grassantis inimici mea simul membra percussa sunt, saevientes gladii per mea viscera transierunt. Immunis et liber a persecutionis incursu fuisse non potest animus. In prostratis fratribus et me prostravit affectus.
pass_a_gloss: Behold, most beloved brothers, peace has been restored to the Church, and what recently seemed impossible to the unbelieving and the faithless, our security has been restored by divine aid and vengeance. Minds return to joy, and with the storm of oppression and the cloud dispersed, tranquility and serenity have shone forth. Praises must be given to God, and His benefits and gifts must be celebrated with thanksgiving, although our voice did not cease to give thanks even in persecution. For the enemy cannot be allowed so much that we, who love the Lord with our whole heart and soul and strength, do not always and everywhere proclaim His blessings and praises with glory. The day longed for by all has come, and after the horrible and gloomy darkness of the long night, the world has shone forth radiant with the Lord's light. We look with joyful gaze upon the confessors, renowned for their good name and glorious for the praises of virtue and faith, clinging to them with holy kisses, embracing those long desired with insatiable longing. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers is present, who broke the ferocity of the turbulent persecution with a stable confrontation, prepared for the patience of prison, armed for the tolerance of death. You resisted the world strongly, you presented a glorious spectacle to God, you were an example to the following brothers. The religious voice spoke Christ, in whom it confessed to have once believed. Illustrious hands, which were accustomed only to divine works, resisted sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly foods, after the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your head remained free from the impious and wicked veil, with which the heads of the captives who sacrificed were veiled. Your forehead, with the sign of God, pure, could not bear the devil's crown, it reserved itself for the Lord's crown. How the mother Church joyfully receives you, returning from battle! How blessed, how rejoicing she opens her gates, so that you may enter with gathered troops, bringing back trophies from the prostrate enemy! Women come with the triumphant men, who, fighting with the world, also overcame their sex. The virgins also come, with the double glory of their military service, and the boys, who spent their years in virtues. The rest of the multitude of the standing also follows your glory, with the closest and almost connected signs of praise, they accompany your footsteps. The same sincerity of heart is in them, the same integrity of tenacious faith. Fixed on the unshaken roots of the heavenly precepts and strengthened by the evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by the prescribed exiles, nor the destined torments, nor the losses of their family, nor the punishments of their body. The days were predetermined for the testing of faith. But he who remembers that he has renounced the world, knows no day of the world; nor does he compute earthly times, who hopes for eternity from God. No one, most beloved brothers, no one must mutilate this glory, no one must weaken the incorrupt firmness of the standing with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those who denied has passed, whoever has not professed within the day has confessed that he is a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, apprehended by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step to glory is to be reserved for the Lord by a cautious secession. The former is a public confession, the latter a private one. The former conquers the judge of the world, the latter, content with his own judge, God, keeps a pure conscience with the integrity of the heart. There, fortitude is more prompt, here solicitude is more secure. He who was already mature when his hour approached, was found; he, perhaps, was delayed who, having abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he was not going to deny: he would have confessed, certainly, if he had also been detained. These heavenly crowns of the martyrs, these spiritual glories of the confessors, these greatest and most excellent virtues of the standing brothers, one sorrow afflicts, that the violent enemy has thrown down a torn part of our bowels with the destruction of his population. What shall I do in this place, most beloved brothers? Fluctuating with a varied storm of the mind, what or how shall I say? Tears are needed more than words to express the grief with which the wound of our body must be lamented, with which the multiple loss of the once numerous people must be mourned. For who is so hard or iron-like, who is so forgetful of fraternal charity, that, established among the many and mournful ruins and the lugubrious and very squalid remnants of his own, he can prevail to keep dry eyes, and not, with the immediate eruption of weeping, pour out his groans in tears rather than in voice? I grieve, brothers, I grieve with you, nor does my own integrity and private health flatter me to alleviate my grief, when the shepherd is more wounded in the wound of his flock. My heart is joined with each one, I participate in the mournful weights of sorrow and funeral. I lament with those who lament, I weep with those who weep, I believe I lie down with those who lie down. The darts of the raging enemy have struck my members at the same time, the raging swords have passed through my bowels. The mind cannot have been immune and free from the attack of persecution. In the prostrate brothers, affection has also prostrated me.

pass_b_english: Behold, dearest brothers, peace has returned to the Church, and by God's own aid and vengeance our security has been restored—something that recently seemed impossible to the unbelieving and the faithless. Minds turn back to joy, and now that the storm of oppression has blown over and the cloud has been dispersed, tranquility and serenity shine forth once more. We must give praise to God and celebrate his benefits and gifts with thanksgiving, even though our voice never stopped giving thanks even during the persecution. For the enemy cannot be given so much power that we—who love the Lord with our whole heart and soul and strength—fail to proclaim his blessings and praises always and everywhere with glory. The day that everyone longed for has come, and after the horrible, gloomy darkness of the long night, the world has shone out radiant with the Lord's light. We look upon the confessors with joyful eyes—men renowned for their good name and glorious in the praise of virtue and faith—clinging to them with holy kisses and embracing those we have longed for with an insatiable desire. The white cohort of Christ's soldiers stands here, those who broke the ferocious turbulence of the persecution by their steadfast stand, ready for the endurance of prison, armed for the endurance of death. You resisted the world mightily; you offered a glorious spectacle to God; you became an example for the brothers who follow. A religious voice confessed Christ, in whom it declared it had once believed. Illustrious hands, accustomed only to divine works, refused to take part in sacrilegious sacrifices. Mouths sanctified by heavenly food, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, rejected profane contagions and the remnants of idols. Your heads remained free from the impious and wicked veil with which the heads of the captive sacrificers were covered. Your foreheads, marked pure with the sign of God, could not bear the devil's crown; they reserved themselves for the Lord's crown. How joyfully mother Church welcomes you, returning from battle! How blessed and rejoicing she opens her gates so that you may enter with gathered ranks, carrying back trophies from the prostrate enemy! Women come alongside the triumphant men—women who, fighting against the world, also conquered their own sex. The virgins come too, bearing the double glory of their warfare, and boys who have spent their years in virtues. The rest of the multitude of the standing follows your glory as well, their insignia of praise so closely joined to yours that they walk in your footsteps. They share the same sincerity of heart, the same integrity of tenacious faith. Rooted in the unshaken roots of the heavenly precepts and strengthened by the evangelical traditions, they were not terrified by prescribed exiles, destined torments, the loss of their family property, or the punishments of their bodies. The days were predetermined for the testing of faith. But whoever remembers that he has renounced the world knows no day of the world; nor does he calculate earthly times, since he hopes for eternity from God. No one, dearest brothers, must mutilate this glory; no one must weaken the incorrupt steadfastness of the standing with malignant detraction. When the day appointed for those who denied had passed, whoever had not professed within that day confessed that he is a Christian. The first title of victory is to confess the Lord, seized by the hands of the Gentiles; the second step toward glory is to be reserved for the Lord by a cautious withdrawal. The former is a public confession, the latter a private one. The former conquers the judge of the world; the latter, content with God as his judge, guards a pure conscience with integrity of heart. In the former, fortitude is more prompt; in the latter, solicitude is more secure. The one was found mature when his hour approached; the other was perhaps delayed—he who, having abandoned his patrimony, withdrew because he would not deny; he would certainly have confessed if he had also been detained. One sorrow afflicts these heavenly crowns of the martyrs, these spiritual glories of the confessors, these greatest and most excellent virtues of the standing brothers: the violent enemy has thrown down a torn part of our own bowels through the slaughter of his people. What shall I do in this place, dearest brothers? My mind tossed by a varied storm, what shall I say, or how? Tears are needed more than words to express the grief with which the wound of our body must be lamented, and the manifold loss of a once numerous people must be mourned. For who is so hard or iron-hearted, who so forgetful of fraternal charity, that standing amid the manifold ruins and the mournful, squalid remnants of his own people he can keep his eyes dry, and not—immediately bursting into weeping—pour out his groans in tears rather than in voice? I grieve, brothers, I grieve with you; my own integrity and private health do not flatter me into easing my grief, when the shepherd is wounded all the more in the wound of his flock. My heart is joined to each of you; I share the mournful weights of sorrow and funeral. I lament with those who lament, I weep with those who weep, I feel that I lie down with those who lie down. The darts of the raging enemy have struck my members at the same time; the raging swords have passed through my own bowels. The mind could not be immune and free from the onslaught of persecution. In my prostrate brothers, affection has prostrated me as well.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the passive constructions (e.g., 'securitas nostra reparata est' -> 'our security has been restored') and the distinction between the public and private confessions. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source and each other.
